panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Radiograph of a child's right hip showing classic head-at-risk signs of Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease including lateral subluxation, lateral epiphyseal calcification, and Gage sign, consistent with lateral pillar classification group C2. B: Pelvic radiograph of an adolescent showing Stulberg IV femoral head deformity with flattening, representing a late-stage outcome of Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease.

panels.figure_caption: (A) An example of a right hip in group C2 of the modified lateral pillar classification in a patient who was 3.2 years old at presentation. This radiograph shows three significant radiographical head-at-risk signs, lateral subluxation of the femoral head, calcification lateral to the epiphysis, Gage's sign and a diffuse metaphyseal reaction. Among them, only three signs were related to the prognosis. (B) Anteroposterior and frog-leg lateral radiograph of the pelvis, made at the age of fifteen years, showing the Stulberg IV femoral head with a marked difference between the two hips. Affected hip shows a flattening of the femoral head.
in_text_mentions: The patients were divided into those with ≤ 1 statistically significant sign and those with ≥ 2 statistically significant signs (Figs. 3-6). There were 19 (45%) hips in the former group. Thirteen (68%) of those were classified as Stulberg I and II hips. There were 20 (51%) hips in the latter group with 18 (90%) of them being classified as Stulberg III, IV, and V hips. Therefore, the final outcome was poorer in those with more head-at-risk signs (Stulberg classification) was (p = 0.001) (Tables 3 and 4).

in_text_mentions: A total number of 39 hips (23 left hips, 16 right hips) in 39 consecutive patients (10 women, 29 men) were retrospectively identified. Catteral grades of these 39 consecutive patients were as follows: Catteral 1 (n = 5), Caterall 2 (n = 6), Catteral 3 (n = 12), and Catteral 4 (n = 11). Preoperative radiographs were missing in 5 cases. In 4 patients hip disease was bilateral, but CPO was performed only on the more affected side, while the contralateral hip was managed conservatively. All patients were routinely followed by clinical and radiological examinations (Figures 1–3).

e femoral head cover percentage (FHC) and Reimer’s Index (RI) were calculated as the horizontal distance of the lateral femoral head covered (A)/uncovered (A’) by the acetabulum divided by the total horizontal width of the femoral head (B). Both indices were expressed as a percentage (Figures 1 and 3).24 Catterall and Herring classifications were used to preoperatively assess the stage of femoral head involvement.2,25 Stulberg classification was applied to evaluate the femoral head condition in radiographic outcomes and summarised as good (I/II), fair (III) or poor (IV/V) postoperatively.26,27

in_text_mentions: s’ mean age at diagnosis was 3.9 (range: 1.9–5.9) years, and the mean follow-up duration was 14.3 (range: 6.2–27.8) years (Table 1). The medical records of all patients were reviewed to extract data on the sex, age of onset, treatment method, and follow-up duration. Moreover, two orthopedic surgeons (HSO and SK) reviewed the standard anteroposterior and frog-leg radiographs of the hips throughout the treatment course (Figure 1). To evaluate disease severity, we applied the lateral pillar classification when the disease showed maximal epiphyseal fragmentation in the fragmentation stage [12,13].

the duration of the stage. We used the modified Waldenström classification published by Joseph et al. [14] to determine the onset of initial, fragmentation, and reossification stages. The onset of the initial stage was defined as the time when part or whole of the epiphysis was sclerotic (Figure 1A). When one or two vertical fissures were present in the anteroposterior or frog-leg lateral view, we marked the onset of the fragmentation stage (Figure 1B). The onset of the reossification stage was defined as the time when early new bone was visible lateral to the fragmented epiphysis (Figure 1C).

The final outcome was evaluated radiographically using the Stulberg classification. The Stulberg class was determined from radiographs at the time of skeletal maturity, and patients without skeletal maturity at the final follow-up were excluded (Figure 1D) [13]. Stulberg classes I and II were considered to be good, III to be fair, and IV and V to be poor.

panels.figure_caption: Imaging showing mild flattening and focal fragmentation of the right femoral head epiphysis (blue arrow) with areas of sclerosis, suggestive of avascular necrosis of the femoral epiphysis (Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease).
in_text_mentions: Incidentally, evaluation of the bone window images revealed mild flattening with focal fragmentation of the right femoral head epiphysis, accompanied by surrounding sclerosis. This was noted as an incidental finding. These imaging features were consistent with avascular necrosis of the femoral head, suggestive of LCPD (Figure 3). On further clinical evaluation, the child had a normal gait with no limping. Hip examination revealed no restriction of movement, and the musculoskeletal findings were clinically asymptomatic at presentation.
